To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
frailty, health and QoL differ between care-dependent community living older people (≥65 years) with and without remaining natural teeth who recently received home care.
older people with remaining dentition are less frail, have better physical functioning and health, and have a better quality of life than edentulous people.
older people with remaining natural teeth are more independent and less frail, have a better quality of life and better physical and general health than edentulous people.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a vulnerable group of elderly people who are in need of extra attention.
the importance of oral health in older people.
the oral and general health of older people with and edentulous people.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
older people with remaining natural teeth have better health and QoL than older people without teeth.
older people with remaining natural teeth, who are living at home and receive home care, have better health and QoL.
oral health, health and QoL of care-dependent older people with remaining dentition are generally better than of those who are edentulous.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
oral health care for the elderly is a shared responsibility of dentists and other health care workers.
oral care should be part of the general health care of older people.
oral health and oral health-related quality of life are important factors for the general well-being of the care-dependent older people.
The main takeaway from our work is that
older people who have remaining teeth are less frail, have better QoL, and are more physically fit.
oral health is not only a matter of oral health care professionals.
oral health is important to health and QoL, even in frail older people.
